title: Sources and reading
text:
Differential games

Tamer Başar and Geert Jan Olsder — Dynamic Noncooperative Game Theory
Reference for dynamic games, information patterns, equilibrium concepts, and pursuit–evasion.


Rufus Isaacs — Differential Games
Classical geometric perspective on differential games and pursuit–evasion.


N. N. Krasovskii and A. I. Subbotin — Game-Theoretical Control Problems
Reference for positional strategies and guaranteed outcomes.


A. A. Chikrii — Conflict-Controlled Processes
Reference for resolving functions, constructive pursuit, and multiplayer problems.


B. N. Pshenichnyi and V. V. Ostapenko — Differential Games
Companion reference for the constructive pursuit tradition.

title: Optimal Control and Differential Games
text:
This course explores how to control dynamical systems and make decisions in the presence of conflict.
We begin with linear optimal control, reachable sets, and minimum-time problems. We then move to pursuit–evasion games with two and more players, constructive pursuit methods, positional strategies, and Hamilton–Jacobi equations.
Mathematical lectures are paired with Python notebooks designed for Google Colab. The notebooks support visualization, numerical experiments, strategy comparisons, and student assignments.
We will also aim for lean formalization.

title: Optimal Control and Differential Games
text:
Learning approach
Each topic follows a common sequence:

Formulate a mathematical problem.
Develop geometric intuition.
Derive a result and examine its assumptions.
Implement a numerical experiment.
Compare methods and identify limitations.

A central theme is the distinction between a successful simulation, an approximate numerical solution, and a mathematically established guarantee.

I am particularly interested in connecting rigorous strategy guarantees with numerical evaluation and learning-based methods.

title: Lecture 1. Formulation of an Optimal Control Problem
text:
2 1. State and control
When we have optimal control problem usually we are working with some object depending on time. At each moment of time this object fully determined by parameters $ (x{1}(t),,x{n}(t))$, which can be coordinates of position, components of velocity etc.
Vector \(\mathbf{x}(t)\) is called the phase state of object: \[
\mathbf{x}(t)=\bigl(x^{1}(t),\ldots,x^{n}(t)\bigr)
\]
We also imply that we can influence the process with some function, usually called control. The control represents quantities that we may choose:
\[
\mathbf{u}(t)=\bigl(u^{1}(t),\ldots,u^{m}(t)\bigr)
\]
It is natural to think that current state of the system depends on previous values of \(\mathbf{u}(t)\) and does not depend on future control.
In this course we will assume a dynamic controlled system has the form:
\[
\dot{\mathbf{x}}=f(t,\mathbf{x},\mathbf{u}).
\tag{1}\]
Once a control and an initial condition are specified, we obtain an initial-value problem, whre trajectory is a solution of differential equation
\[
\dot{\mathbf{x}(t)}=f(t,\mathbf{x}(t),\mathbf{u}(t)).
\]






NoteStanding assumption



In the examples considered here, we assume that the chosen control produces a well-defined, unique trajectory on the interval under consideration.

title: Lecture 1. Formulation of an Optimal Control Problem
text:
3 2. Admissible controls
Controls cannot usually be chosen arbitrarily.
We impose
\[
u(t)\in U.
\tag{2}\]
For a scalar bounded input, an example is
\[
U=[-1,1].
\]
In this lecture’s computational experiments, we use piecewise-constant controls. More general admissible control classes will be discussed later.

3.1 Question
Why should the admissible class of controls be specified before solving an optimization problem?

title: Lecture 1. Formulation of an Optimal Control Problem
text:
4 3. Initial and terminal conditions
Let \(M_0\) be the initial set and \(M_1\) the terminal set.
A transfer must satisfy
\[
x(t_0)\in M_0,
\qquad
x(t_1)\in M_1.
\tag{3}\]
An important special case is
\[
M_0=\{x_0\},
\qquad
M_1=\{x_{\mathrm{target}}\}.
\]
A feasible control satisfies the control constraints and produces a trajectory meeting the boundary conditions.
Finding a feasible control is not the same as finding an optimal control.

title: Lecture 1. Formulation of an Optimal Control Problem
text:
5 4. The objective functional
Among feasible controls, we may seek one minimizing
\[
J(u)=
\int_{t_0}^{t_1}
f^0(s,x(s),u(s))\,ds.
\tag{4}\]
For example, choosing \(f^0=1\) gives
\[
J(u)=t_1-t_0.
\]
When the terminal time is free, this leads to a minimum-time problem.

5.1 Questions

Is the terminal time fixed or free?
Is the terminal condition an equality or a set constraint?
Does an admissible control necessarily reach the target?
Is an optimal control guaranteed to exist?

title: Lecture 1. Formulation of an Optimal Control Problem
text:
6 5. Example: a controlled harmonic oscillator
Consider the normalized mechanical system
\[
\ddot y+y=u,
\qquad |u|\le1.
\tag{5}\]
Introduce
\[
x_1=y,
\qquad
x_2=\dot y.
\]
Then
\[
\begin{aligned}
\dot x_1 &= x_2,\\
\dot x_2 &= -x_1+u.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}\]
Equivalently,
\[
\dot x=Ax+Bu,
\qquad
A=
\begin{pmatrix}
0&1\\
-1&0
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
B=
\begin{pmatrix}
0\\
1
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
A control problem is to transfer a prescribed initial state \(x_0\) to the origin in minimum time.

title: Lecture 1. Formulation of an Optimal Control Problem
text:
7 6. Computational experiment
Before solving the optimal-control problem, compare several admissible controls:

\(u(t)=0\);
\(u(t)=1\);
\(u(t)=-1\);
a control that switches once between its extreme values.

Plot:

The control history.
Position and velocity versus time.
The trajectory in the state plane.







WarningInterpretation



These experiments compare candidate controls. They do not establish that any candidate is optimal.

title: Lecture 1. Formulation of an Optimal Control Problem
text:
8 7. The linear minimum-time problem
The course will study linear controlled systems of the form
\[
\dot x=Ax+u,
\qquad u(t)\in U,
\]
and transfers from an initial set to a terminal set in minimum time.
In applications it is also convenient to write
\[
\dot x=Ax+Bv,
\qquad v(t)\in V.
\]
Here the admissible forcing set in the first notation can be taken as \(U=BV\).
The next lectures develop the mathematical tools needed to analyze such problems.

title: Lecture 1. Formulation of an Optimal Control Problem
text:
9 Exercises

Rewrite \(\ddot y+y=u\) as a first-order system.
Identify the state, control set, initial set, terminal set, and objective for the oscillator problem.
Explain why \(u(t)=0\) cannot transfer a nonzero oscillator state to the origin.
For a constant control \(u=a\), determine the equilibrium.
Show that trajectories under constant \(a\) satisfy
\[
(x_1-a)^2+x_2^2=\text{constant}.
\]
Compare a minimum-time objective with a fixed-time minimum-energy objective.

title: Course outline
text: This preliminary outline combines mathematical reading, lectures, and computational laboratories. The pace and selection of advanced topics may change as the materials develop.

title: Course outline
section: Part I. Foundations of optimal control
text:
Part I. Foundations of optimal control

1. Controlled dynamical systems

States, controls, and admissible trajectories.
Linear systems and the solution formula.
Exact propagation under piecewise-constant controls.

Laboratory: simulate the integrator and double integrator; compare analytical and numerical trajectories.
Lecture 1. Formulation of an Optimal Control Problem


2. Reachable sets and controllability

Fixed-time reachable sets.
Convex geometry and supporting directions.
Controllability versus bounded-control reachability.

Laboratory: construct reachable sets, explore their boundaries, and test target feasibility.


3. Minimum-time control

Earliest arrival at a target.
Bang-bang controls and switching geometry.
Analytical reference solutions.

Laboratory: solve the double-integrator minimum-time problem and compare analytical and numerical results.


4. Objectives and numerical optimization

Minimum time, minimum energy, and tracking.
Terminal constraints and penalty formulations.
Discretized controls and numerical optimization.

Laboratory: compare objectives under the same dynamics and control constraints.

title: Course outline
section: Part II. From optimal control to differential games
text:
Part II. From optimal control to differential games

5. Adversarial control

Pursuer and evader objectives.
Controls, feedback policies, and information patterns.
Guaranteed outcomes versus optimal outcomes.



6. Constructive pursuit methods

Pontryagin’s direct pursuit methods.
Pshenychnyi and group pursuit.
Chikrii’s resolving-functions approach.
Sufficient capture conditions and guaranteed-time bounds.



7. Positional strategies

Krasovskii–Subbotin framework.
Stable bridges and extremal aiming.
Numerical approximation and strategy realization.

title: Course outline
section: Part III. Value functions and computation
text:
Part III. Value functions and computation

8. Dynamic programming and Hamilton–Jacobi equations

HJB and HJI formulations.
Boundary and terminal conditions.
Verification and nonsmooth value functions.



9. Strategy evaluation

Common benchmark problems.
Opponent collections and approximate best responses.
Sensitivity, discretization, and reproducibility.

title: Course outline
text:
Part IV. Learning-based methods

10. Learning controllers and value functions

Supervised approximation of known solutions.
Closed-loop evaluation.
Neural value-function approximation.
Adversarial training and its limitations.
